title: European standards of prevention and care: Module on antenatal screening for HIV, hepatitis B and syphilis

analysis.location_and_population: The European Union/European Economic Area (EU/EEA) is the location. The population includes pregnant and breastfeeding individuals, particularly those at risk of vertical transmission, and data on live births and chronic/acute hepatitis B cases are provided.
analysis.event: The event is the development of European standards for antenatal screening for HIV, hepatitis B, and syphilis, including data on vertical transmission rates. The report is published by the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC) and the European AIDS Clinical Society (EACS).
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: In 2024, 196 newly diagnosed HIV infections in the EU/EEA were reported as resulting from vertical transmission, with 75% among migrants. For congenital syphilis, there were 140 confirmed cases in 28 EU/EEA countries. For hepatitis B, 1% of acute cases were due to vertical transmission, and 39% of chronic cases had vertical transmission as the most common route, though 91% were classified as imported.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: The report outlines the development of standards of care for HIV, hepatitis B, and syphilis, including quality statements and outcome indicators. It is based on scientific rationale and current guidelines. The data on vertical transmission are reported, but the completeness of data for hepatitis B is noted as limited.

analysis.brief_en: The European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC) and the European AIDS Clinical Society (EACS) have developed standards of care for antenatal screening of HIV, hepatitis B, and syphilis. These standards aim to prevent vertical transmission and ensure equitable, high-quality care for pregnant and breastfeeding individuals. In 2024, 196 newly diagnosed HIV infections in the EU/EEA were reported as resulting from vertical transmission, with 75% among migrants. There were 140 confirmed congenital syphilis cases in 28 EU/EEA countries, corresponding to a notification rate of 4.7 per 100,000 live births. For hepatitis B, only 1% of acute cases in 2023 were due to vertical transmission, and 39% of chronic cases had vertical transmission as the most common route, though 91% were classified as imported. The report highlights the importance of comprehensive data collection and the need for improved reporting mechanisms to better understand and address vertical transmission risks. The standards are based on scientific rationale, best practices, and ethical considerations, with a focus on accessibility and non-discrimination.

analysis.event: A study published by Xia & He Publishing Inc. highlights the molecular basis and clinical significance of the high-risk phenotype of hepatitis B virus genotype C, emphasizing its association with delayed HBeAg seroconversion, persistent viral replication, active inflammation, faster fibrosis progression, and higher risk of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC).
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: Genotype C is associated with increased HCC risk compared to genotype B (HR ≈ 2.35; meta-analysis OR ≈ 2.05). It also features persistent replication, delayed HBeAg seroconversion, and a higher likelihood of developing cirrhosis and HCC, even after antiviral suppression.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: The study discusses the clinical implications of genotype C as a risk-enhancing virological factor. analysis.brief_en: A study published on 24-Sep-2026 by Xia & He Publishing Inc. explores the high-risk phenotype of hepatitis B virus genotype C, highlighting its clinical relevance.
